title: Northshore Capital - Data Stewardship & Request Storage Toggle Demo
summary: Demo focused on console + API controls for request storage, redaction, PII detection and retention policies. Customer wanted specifics about retention by environment, per-route overrides, exportability of audit logs, and compatibility with KMS/SAML. Agreed next steps: send security pack, schedule a 2-week pilot for dedicated ephemeral retention, and run a small benchmark on sample workloads.
action_items: Tom Waller|Share SOC2 + Incident Response + data flow diagram|2026-11-09
Sofia Nguyen|Prepare POC plan: 2-week ephemeral pilot + sample request set|2026-11-10
Lena Ortiz|Provide sample request patterns and top 5 endpoints to test|2026-11-08
next_steps: Redwood to share security pack and console recording
Customer to confirm pilot scope and provide sample payloads
Run a quick cost/latency baseline on provided sample traffic
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-11-05 15:00 UTC | Duration: 48m | Attendees: Tom, Sofia, Maya (Redwood) — Rajesh, Lena, Mark, Evan (Northshore)

[00:00] Tom Waller: hi everybody, thanks for joining, i'm tom from redwood, i'll kick off — this is a focused demo on how we handle request storage and PII redaction in both the console and via the api. Sofia and Maya are with me — Sofia's going to walk through the console flows.

[00:22] Rajesh Iyer: hey all, quick context — at northshore we have strict retention needs for trading PII, we can't keep request text longer than necessary and we need auditability for regulators, SOC 2 plus some internal checks. we're evaluating hosted vs dedicated and particularly how we can guarantee that certain routes never persist user text.

[00:45] Sofia Nguyen: totally, that makes sense. i'll start in the console — so this is the request storage page, you can see a global toggle, and then per-route overrides. if global is off, nothing is persisted except minimal telemetry, but you can still enable route-level ephemeral capture for debugging for a limited window.

[01:12] Lena Ortiz: when you say "nothing is persisted" — what about logs and audit trails? we need to keep traces for 90 days for investigations.

[01:20] Sofia Nguyen: good question, so we separate request storage from audit logging. audit logs contain metadata — timestamps, request IDs, model used, which route — but they do not contain full request text if storage is off. you can choose to redact personally identifiable entities in audit logs too.

[01:40] Maya Patel: i'll show the redaction policy editor — you can pick automatic PII detection (names, emails, ssn-like patterns) using our NER detector, or you can supply custom regex rules. applied policies support tiers: remove, mask, or hash. for example you can mask account numbers but keep last 4 digits.

[02:05] Mark Chen: do you support custom classifiers? we have internal identifiers that don't match common patterns.

[02:12] Maya Patel: yes — you can upload a small training set or provide a list of tokens to be treated as PII or sensitive. the policy engine will run a fast lookup before redaction. note there can be some false positives/negatives — we recommend a short evaluation period.

[02:35] [02:39] Evan Brooks: latency impact? if we run redaction inline will that add overhead per request?

[02:43] Sofia Nguyen: inline redaction adds a small CPU step — typically 5-15ms for standard NER on text sized like chat messages. if you're on dedicated GPU pools you can offload redaction to pre-processing workers or use async ephemeral capture so generation isn't blocked.

[03:05] Tom Waller: another pattern is prefix/KV caching so you don't repeatedly analyze the same tokens; that reduces cost and latency in production.

[03:20] Rajesh Iyer: and for regulatory audits we have to export logs to our SIEM. can you ingest to S3 or forward via Kinesis?

[03:29] Sofia Nguyen: yes — audit logs are exportable via S3, and you can configure push to an HTTP endpoint or a streaming service. all exports can be encrypted with customer KMS keys.

[03:45] Lena Ortiz: about encryption — are request bodies stored encrypted and who manages the keys?

[03:50] Maya Patel: storage at rest is always encrypted; for hosted customers we can either use Redwood-managed keys or your own KMS (AWS KMS/HSM) in a bring-your-own-key model. note that with BYOK we also provide key rotation notices and integration docs.

[04:10] Mark Chen: what about SSO and admin role separation? we need RBAC so only certain teams can disable retention.

[04:16] Sofia Nguyen: console integrates with SAML/SSO and supports fine-grained RBAC; you can lock critical toggles behind admin-only permissions and require an approval workflow for changes.

[04:30] Rajesh Iyer: can you show per-route override examples? we have /payments and /customer_chat which need different policies.

[04:38] Sofia Nguyen: sure — here's the route config for /payments: request storage off, redaction policy set to remove PAN-like tokens and hash account ids. /customer_chat is ephemeral on with 48-hour retention for debugging, everything else redacted. you can also set per-environment defaults (prod vs staging).

[05:05] [05:08] Lena Ortiz: is the ephemeral window configurable? we might want 24h for prod and 7 days for staging.

[05:12] Maya Patel: yes, windows are configurable to the minute — you can also set hard caps so developers can't extend beyond org policy.

[05:28] Evan Brooks: curious about billing impact — storing requests for 7 days vs 90 days, how does that change cost?

[05:34] Tom Waller: roughly it's linear to storage and egress; Optimize has a calculator that estimates cost per token based on retention. for short windows the delta is minimal compared to inference cost; long retention >90d starts to be material. we'll share a baseline after the pilot.

[05:52] Rajesh Iyer: show me the API route for toggles — we want infra automation.

[05:56] Sofia Nguyen: here — /v1/orgs/{org_id}/settings/request_storage with JSON payload {"enabled":false,"default_retention_days":0}. you can patch per-route with /v1/orgs/{org_id}/routes/{route_id}/retention. responses are standard 200/400/401.

[06:20] Mark Chen: how do you prevent accidental enabling by devs? we need approval flows.

[06:25] Sofia Nguyen: we have an approvals API and a console workflow; toggles can be flagged as "admin locked" which requires SSO group membership and optional 2-step approval.

[06:40] [06:44] Rajesh Iyer: audit trails — if someone flips a toggle we need a tamper-proof record.

[06:47] Maya Patel: audit records include who, when, before/after and are hashed and signed. We keep immutable logs for configured retention and you can forward them to your SIEM.

[07:05] Evan Brooks: about private deployments — if we go private/on-prem does the same console exist?

[07:11] Tom Waller: yes, for Private we ship a control plane that can be customer-managed in a VPC. policies are enforced locally and you can integrate with your KMS and SSO. dedicated capacity has the same APIs and console features.

[07:30] Rajesh Iyer: any differences in redaction behavior between hosted and private?

[07:34] Maya Patel: functionality is the same; the only difference is where keys and logs live. with on-prem you keep complete custody of logs and keys.

[07:48] [08:00] Sofia Nguyen: quick demo of the Optimize suggestions — the system suggests turning on prefix caching for routes with repeated prompts, and suggests lower quantization for internal workloads. for retention it suggests switching staging to ephemeral for 7 days and turning prod to off with audit-only mode.

[08:25] Lena Ortiz: show me an example of redaction failure — how do we detect regressions?

[08:30] Maya Patel: we have a sampling and eval pipeline — you can add a small eval set with expected redactions and the system will alert if redaction rates drop. it's part of the quality monitoring.

[08:50] Mark Chen: important — we need demonstrable proof that sensitive tokens are scrubbed in exported logs. can you run a scrub-and-export test?

[08:58] Sofia Nguyen: yes, during pilot we'll run a scrubbed export to your S3 and show sample objects. we can also provide a signed certificate after export for audit.

[09:15] Rajesh Iyer: what about legal holds — we might need to retain a subset of data beyond normal policy for investigations. can you do fine-grained holds?

[09:24] Maya Patel: yes — legal hold is supported per-request-id or per-route and you can query holds via API. holds override retention but are surfaced in the audits.

[09:40] Evan Brooks: could you recap how we should architect for low latency and zero-persist for production?

[09:46] Tom Waller: recommended pattern: set global request storage off for prod, enable audit-only logs, use per-route ephemeral for dev with 24h to 7d, offload NER to pre-processors where needed, and use caching to avoid repeated analysis. if you need worst-case low latency, route to a smaller model variant or a dedicated pool.

[10:12] Rajesh Iyer: about PII detection accuracy — do you publish false positive/negative rates?

[10:17] Maya Patel: we publish internal benchmarks for common entity types — names, emails, credit-card-ish patterns. for custom tokens, accuracy depends on training data; we recommend a short evaluation during POC.

[10:35] Lena Ortiz: any gotchas with GDPR and data exports?

[10:39] Sofia Nguyen: exports are subject to the same retention rules; if a user requests erasure, we have a process to delete corresponding request text provided it's not under legal hold. for GDPR you can set per-region retention and data residency controls.

[10:58] Mark Chen: if we run in dedicated mode, is there any shared metadata that could leak org ids or patterns?

[11:05] Tom Waller: in Dedicated we guarantee tenant isolation and no cross-tenant model caching of secrets. metadata is scoped to org; we do not co-mingle request content.

[11:22] Rajesh Iyer: timeline — we'd like a pilot next week if possible. what do you need from us?

[11:26] Sofia Nguyen: sample payloads, a list of routes and expected retention per route, and a point-of-contact for access. we'll provision a sandbox dedicated pool and run the pilot.

[11:38] Evan Brooks: quick note — are there limits on number of per-route rules? we have a lot of microservices.

[11:44] Maya Patel: no practical limit; we recommend grouping similar routes under policy templates to keep it manageable.

[12:00] [12:05] Rajesh Iyer: safety — is there a way to require manual review for flagged outputs before they return to users?

[12:10] Sofia Nguyen: yes — you can enable a review queue where flagged responses are held and surfaced in a reviewer UI or forwarded to a webhook for your moderation system.

[12:25] Tom Waller: ok, let's do a short live scenario — Sofia can flip the /customer_chat route to ephemeral and show the export.

[12:30] Sofia Nguyen: flipping it now... done, changed to ephemeral 48h. check logs — you can see request id 9b3f... created and marked ephemeral. i'll run a small sample message.

[12:50] [13:00] Sofia Nguyen: sample message posted, the UI shows it redacted — name masked, email hashed. exporting to S3 now — link will appear in a minute.

[13:20] Rajesh Iyer: i noticed the redaction replaced the name with [REDACTED] not a token — can we preserve token mapping for pseudo-anonymization?

[13:27] Maya Patel: yes — choose hash mode and include a salt from your KMS so mapping is non-reversible without the key.

[13:40] Mark Chen: about evidence for auditors — can we produce a report that shows before/after with hashes?

[13:45] Sofia Nguyen: we can export a redaction report that contains hashed tokens and show sampling of requests with timestamps.

[14:00] [14:10] Rajesh Iyer: any rate limits on export? we need bulk export for a few TBs if required for legal.

[14:16] Maya Patel: exports are chunked; we support bulk exports but for very large jobs we coordinate to avoid operational impacts. there's a process in the runbook.

[14:35] Evan Brooks: last question — if we want ephemeral + encrypted in transit to our VPC, how is that wired?

[14:41] Tom Waller: we can set up private peering or run Private control plane inside your VPC; traffic can use TLS and mutual auth, and logs go straight to your S3 via VPC gateway.

[14:58] [15:00] Tom Waller: great, that's our walkthrough — to recap: we'll share security pack and console recording, run a 2-week ephemeral pilot scoped to routes you provide, and do a scrubbed export to your S3 for audit.

[15:18] Rajesh Iyer: perfect. i'll get the payloads to Lena and we'll confirm kickoff. thanks everyone.

[15:28] Tom Waller: thanks all — action items in chat, we'll follow up via email.

[15:36] [END]
